lessons.title: African nationalism after 1945
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 4 — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain the causes of the growth of African nationalism
Name key events in the road to independence
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: Ghana's independence date (1957), the 1945 Manchester Congress, and the wording 'first in sub-Saharan Africa' (strictly, Ghana was the first British colony in black Africa to gain independence).

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: **Nationalism** is the desire of a people to rule themselves and to be free of foreign control. **Decolonisation** is the process by which colonies became independent. After 1945 African nationalism grew quickly. Many Africans wanted **political freedom, equality, better education, fair pay** and an end to forced labour, taxes and racial discrimination.

blocks.caption: Road to independence
blocks.alt: A timeline from 1945 to 1965 with 1945, 1957, 1960 and 1963.

blocks.title: Causes
blocks.md:
- **The Second World War**: African soldiers saw colonial powers weakened and had been told the war was for freedom.
- **Education**: schools produced educated Africans who read about freedom and rights.
- **Ideas**: the Atlantic Charter, the UN Charter and **Pan-Africanism** (the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester).
- **Examples abroad**: India and other Asian countries gained independence in the late 1940s.
- **Economic hardship** and dislike of colonial taxes and forced labour.

blocks.title: Methods and events
blocks.md: Nationalists formed **political parties** and **trade unions**, held meetings, wrote in **newspapers**, organised **strikes and boycotts**, petitioned governments and took part in **elections**. In some places there were armed struggles, in others peaceful negotiations. **Ghana** (the Gold Coast) became independent in **1957**, the first black African colony in the south of the Sahara to do so; **1960** is called the **'Year of Africa'** because many colonies became independent.

Colonial powers also changed: after the war Britain and France gave Africans some **political rights**, such as places in councils and assemblies, but at first these were limited. Colonial powers were also costly to maintain and under pressure from the UN and from public opinion. By the mid-1960s most of Africa had become independent, although some colonies fought long wars or waited until later.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Nationalism did not begin suddenly in 1945; it built on earlier protests and resistance, but it grew faster after the war.
- Independence was not always won by war: many countries gained it by negotiation.
- 'Year of Africa' refers to 1960, not 1957.

blocks.title: Example 1: causes
blocks.statement: Give two reasons why the Second World War encouraged nationalism in Africa.
steps: African soldiers served abroad and saw that colonial powers could be defeated.
The Allies spoke of freedom and self-determination.
These ideas encouraged demands for independence.
blocks.answer: Soldiers' experience and the language of freedom.

blocks.title: Example 2: methods
blocks.statement: Name two peaceful methods nationalists used.
steps: They held meetings, wrote newspapers and took part in elections.
Strikes and petitions were also used.

objectives: Describe the growth of nationalism in French Cameroun
Describe political developments in British Southern Cameroons
Name the main parties and organisations
Explain the role of the United Nations
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: party names and founding dates (exact years of the KNC, KPP, KNDP and CPNC are deliberately vague; UPC 1948; ban in 1955; Cameroons Youth League 1940; KNC, KPP, KNDP, CPNC), the 1954 regional status, and the neutral wording about contested events; no individual politicians are named on purpose.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: In **French Cameroun** the main nationalist party was the **Union des Populations du Cameroun (UPC)**, founded in **1948**, which called for **independence and reunification** of the two Cameroons. Other parties and groups also formed as political life opened up after 1945. The UPC was banned in **1955** after unrest, and its leaders went underground or abroad, which led to a period of violence and conflict in some areas before and after independence.

blocks.caption: Some political parties
blocks.alt: Two columns naming parties in French Cameroun and in the Southern Cameroons.

blocks.title: British Cameroons
blocks.md: In the **British Southern Cameroons**, early organisations included the **Cameroons Youth League** (from 1940) and later political parties: the **Kamerun National Congress (KNC)**, the **Kamerun People's Party (KPP)** and the **Kamerun National Democratic Party (KNDP)**, with the **Cameroon Peoples National Convention (CPNC)** later. Their leaders argued about whether to join Nigeria, join French Cameroun, or have another solution.

In **1954** the Southern Cameroons obtained a **separate regional government** and a **House of Assembly** at Buea, with quasi-federal status in Nigeria. Elections to this house, held in the 1950s, were important steps. **Northern Cameroons** remained administered with Northern Nigeria. The **United Nations**, as supervisor of the trusteeship, sent visiting missions, discussed petitions and in the end arranged the plebiscites.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- The two Cameroons followed different political paths because of different colonial administrations.
- Historians and Cameroonians hold different views about these events; present them neutrally and use evidence.
- Do not mix up party names: UPC (French Cameroun) versus KNC, KPP, KNDP and CPNC (British Cameroons).

blocks.title: Example 1: parties
blocks.statement: Name the nationalist party founded in French Cameroun in 1948 and one party from the Southern Cameroons.
steps: Southern Cameroons parties included the KNC and the KNDP.
So UPC and, for example, KNDP.
blocks.answer: UPC; and for example KNC or KNDP.

blocks.title: Example 2: the role of the UN
blocks.statement: How did the UN supervise the trust territories?
steps: It received reports from Britain and France.
It sent visiting missions to the territories.
It also considered petitions and arranged the plebiscites.
blocks.answer: By reports, visiting missions, petitions and plebiscites.
